sections.el: Οι ουδέτερες σειρές: ΥΡΑ και ΡΥΑ
sections.title: The neutral orders: SVO and VSO

body.p: The most neutral order is **subject, verb, object** (ΥΡΑ: υποκείμενο, ρήμα, αντικείμενο), as in English. It answers the question "What happened?" with everything new.

ex.en: The children are playing in the garden.

body.p: **Verb, subject, object** (ΡΥΑ) is just as natural, especially in speech and in news reports, and it is the usual order when the subject is new information or when the verb is "happen, arrive, appear, ring, die" and the like.

ex.en: Giannis has come. / Giannis is here.
The schools have closed because of snow.

head: Order
Example
When it sounds natural
rows: The default: the subject is what we talk about.
Narration, news; the whole event is new.
Verbs of arriving, appearing, happening: the subject is the news.

body.tip: Do not translate "There is / There are" with a dummy subject. Greek simply puts the verb first: **Υπάρχει ένα πρόβλημα** "There is a problem", **Ήρθαν πολλοί** "A lot of people came".

check.q: "The bus has arrived!" (the bus is the news):
check.why: With verbs of arriving the subject comfortably follows the verb.

check.q: "The schools closed." (news headline order, verb first)
check.why: Verb first, then the subject: the whole event is new.

check.q: "Maria is reading a book." (neutral, subject first)
check.why: SVO, as in English.

body.p: The verb ending already says who the subject is, so Greek normally leaves out subject pronouns: **Διαβάζω** "I read", **Ήρθαν** "They came". A subject pronoun is added only to **contrast** or **emphasise**.

ex.en: Where do you live? I live in Athens.

ex.el: Εγώ μένω στην Αθήνα, εσύ πού μένεις;
ex.en: I live in Athens; where do *you* live?

body.p: The pronoun can stand before or after the verb. After the verb it is often even more emphatic: **Θα το κάνω εγώ** "*I'll* do it (not you)".

body.tip: Saying **Εγώ είμαι ο Πέτρος** every time you introduce yourself sounds as if you are correcting someone ("*I* am Petros"). The neutral form is **Είμαι ο Πέτρος** or **Με λένε Πέτρο**.

check.q: Neutral answer to "Τι κάνεις;"
check.why: No contrast, so no pronoun. Καλά είμαι, with καλά first, is the everyday answer.

check.q: "*I'll* pay (not you)!"
check.why: The strong pronoun after the verb marks contrast.

body.p: Every sentence has a part that links to what we already know (the **topic**, θέμα) and a part that brings something new or contrasted (the **focus**, εστίαση). Greek usually puts the topic **first** and the new information **last**.

ex.el: Το βιβλίο το έγραψε ο Καζαντζάκης.
ex.en: The book was written by Kazantzakis. (We were talking about the book; the new part is the author.)
Kazantzakis wrote the book. (We were talking about Kazantzakis.)

body.p: Notice the **το** in the first example. When the object comes first as a topic, Greek repeats it with a weak pronoun just before the verb. This is called **clitic doubling** (κλιτικός διπλασιασμός), and it is the key to Greek word order.

head: Sentence
What is known
What is new
rows: Τον Μιχάλη τον δάγκωσε ο σκύλος.
Τον Μιχάλη τον δάγκωσε χθες ο σκύλος.

body.p: Use the passive less than English does. Where English says "The book was written by Kazantzakis", Greek usually keeps the active verb and fronts the object with its doubling pronoun: **Το βιβλίο το έγραψε ο Καζαντζάκης**.

check.q: We are talking about the cake. "Grandma made it."
options: Την τούρτα την έκανε η γιαγιά.
check.answer: Την τούρτα την έκανε η γιαγιά.
check.why: The cake is the topic: fronted and doubled with την. The new part, η γιαγιά, comes last.

check.q: "As for the car, my father sold it."
check.answer: Το αυτοκίνητο το πούλησε ο πατέρας μου.
check.why: Topic first, doubled with το; the new information (my father) last.

check.q: Make **το κρασί** the topic: Ο Νίκος έφερε το κρασί.
check.answer: Το κρασί το έφερε ο Νίκος.
check.why: Front the object and add the doubling pronoun το; the subject moves to the end as the new information.

sections.title: Contrastive focus: fronting without a pronoun

body.p: If you front the object **without** a doubling pronoun, and stress it, the object becomes the **focus**: it is the new or contrasted part, as in English "It was the WINE that Nikos brought (not the bread)".

ex.el: ΤΟ ΚΡΑΣΙ έφερε ο Νίκος, όχι το ψωμί.
ex.en: It was the wine Nikos brought, not the bread.

ex.el: Το κρασί το έφερε ο Νίκος.
ex.en: The wine, Nikos brought it. (the wine is the topic; Nikos is the news)

ex.el: ΣΤΗ ΘΕΣΣΑΛΟΝΙΚΗ πάμε, όχι στην Αθήνα.
ex.en: It's Thessaloniki we're going to, not Athens.

head: Fronted object
With doubling pronoun
Without doubling pronoun
rows: ΤΟΝ ΓΙΑΝΝΗ είδα, όχι τον Πέτρο.

body.p: The same holds for indirect objects: **Του Γιάννη του δώσανε αύξηση** "Giannis, they gave him a raise" (topic) against **ΤΟΥ ΓΙΑΝΝΗ δώσανε αύξηση** "It was Giannis they gave a raise to" (focus).

body.tip: A fronted **indefinite** object (**ένα αυτοκίνητο, κάτι, τίποτα**) is normally focus, so it takes no doubling pronoun: **Κάτι άκουσα** "I heard something", **Τίποτα δεν είδα** "I saw nothing".

check.q: "It's the RED one I want, not the blue one."
options: Το κόκκινο το θέλω, όχι το μπλε.
ΤΟ ΚΟΚΚΙΝΟ θέλω, όχι το μπλε.
Θέλω το το κόκκινο, όχι το μπλε.
check.answer: ΤΟ ΚΟΚΚΙΝΟ θέλω, όχι το μπλε.
check.why: Contrastive focus: fronted and stressed, no doubling pronoun.

check.q: Which sentence treats **τη Μαρία** as already known?
check.why: The doubling pronoun την marks the fronted object as the topic.

check.q: "It's Thessaloniki we're going to, not Athens."
check.answer: Στη Θεσσαλονίκη πάμε, όχι στην Αθήνα.
check.why: The contrasted place goes first, with no pronoun.

sections.el: Δεξιά μετάθεση: το λέω στο τέλος
sections.title: Right dislocation: adding the topic at the end

body.p: The topic can also come **after** the sentence, as an afterthought, again with a doubling pronoun before the verb. This is very common in speech.

ex.el: Της το είπες της μάνας σου;
ex.en: Did you tell her, your mother?

body.p: In the last example there is no object at all: the subject **η ταινία** simply comes at the end because the speaker's emphasis is on **πολύ μου άρεσε**.

body.tip: Doubling with a pronoun after the verb is a feature of conversation. In formal writing prefer the plain order: **Γνωρίζω το τραγούδι.**

check.q: Everyday spoken Greek for "Have you read it, the book I gave you?"
options: Διάβασες το βιβλίο το που σου έδωσα;
Το διάβασες το βιβλίο που σου έδωσα;
Το διάβασες βιβλίο που σου έδωσα;
check.answer: Το διάβασες το βιβλίο που σου έδωσα;
check.why: The pronoun το before the verb anticipates the object named at the end.

check.q: "Did you see him, Nikos?"
check.why: Pronoun before the verb, the full noun phrase at the end.

body.p: In questions with a question word (τι, ποιος, πού, πότε, πώς, γιατί), the question word comes **first** and the subject usually comes **after the verb**.
A topic can stand **before** the question word: **Ο Γιάννης τι έκανε;** "And Giannis, what did he do?" This is the natural way to switch to a new person or thing in conversation.
A preposition always travels with its question word. Greek never leaves the preposition at the end as English does ("Who did you speak to?").

ex.el: Για ποιο θέμα είναι η συνάντηση;

body.p: Yes/no questions keep the statement order and change only the intonation: **Έρχεται ο Νίκος;** "Is Nikos coming?"

check.q: "Who are you going with?"
check.why: The preposition moves to the front with ποιον.

check.q: "Where does your brother work?"
check.why: After the question word, the verb, then the subject.

check.q: "What is the meeting about?"
check.answer: Για ποιο θέμα είναι η συνάντηση;
check.why: Preposition + question word at the front.

sections.el: Η σειρά στη φράση του ονόματος
sections.title: Order inside the noun phrase

body.p: Adjectives normally come **before** the noun: **ένα μεγάλο σπίτι**. An adjective after the noun, with the article repeated, adds emphasis or contrast: **το σπίτι το μεγάλο** "the big house (not the small one)".
The weak possessive pronoun (μου, σου, του ...) goes after the noun, or after the first adjective:

A genitive noun normally follows the noun it belongs to: **το σπίτι του Νίκου** "Nikos's house". Placed first, it is emphatic: **του Νίκου το σπίτι** "*Nikos's* house". Demonstratives need the article: **αυτό το σπίτι** or **το σπίτι αυτό** "this house".

links.title: Where adjectives go, and what they do
Possessives: μου, σου and ο δικός μου

check.q: "this book"
check.why: A demonstrative needs the article as well.

check.q: "my old friend"
check.why: The weak possessive may follow the first adjective.

check.q: "this new house of mine"
check.why: Demonstrative, article, adjective, then μου (before or after the noun).

sections.el: Βάρος και ρυθμός στον γραπτό λόγο
sections.title: Weight and rhythm in written Greek

body.p: In careful writing, word order follows three habits.

list: **Heavy last.** A long subject or object goes at the end: **Ανακοινώθηκαν χθες τα αποτελέσματα των εξετάσεων για την εισαγωγή στα πανεπιστήμια.**

**Given before new.** Each sentence starts from something already mentioned and ends with the new idea, so the text flows: **Η ανεργία μειώθηκε. Τη μείωση αυτή οι αναλυτές την αποδίδουν στον τουρισμό.**
**Adverbials of time and place frame the sentence.** They often open it: **Το 1830 η Ελλάδα αναγνωρίστηκε ως ανεξάρτητο κράτος.**

body.p: Formal Greek uses clitic doubling less than speech, but a fronted, doubled object is perfectly at home in good journalism: **Το μέτρο αυτό η κυβέρνηση το είχε εξαγγείλει από τον Μάιο.**

Verb-initial sentences are typical of headlines and news leads: **Σε ύφεση εισέρχεται η οικονομία** (the focus phrase first, then the verb, then the subject), **Ψηφίστηκε το νομοσχέδιο για την παιδεία.**

ex.el: Στις 25 Μαρτίου 1821 ξεκίνησε, σύμφωνα με την παράδοση, η Επανάσταση.
ex.en: On 25 March 1821, according to tradition, the Revolution began.

ex.el: Τις αλλαγές αυτές τις ζητούσαν εδώ και χρόνια οι κάτοικοι.
ex.en: The residents had been asking for these changes for years.

links.title: Nominal style: from «επειδή αυξήθηκαν οι τιμές» to «η αύξηση των τιμών»
Register shifting: φτιάχνω → συντάσσω, βγάζω → εκδίδω, είναι → αποτελεί
Argument structure: αρχικά, εκ πρώτης όψεως, εντούτοις, εν κατακλείδι

check.q: A news lead: "The education bill was passed."
options: Το νομοσχέδιο για την παιδεία ψηφίστηκε από τη Βουλή χθες.
Ψηφίστηκε το νομοσχέδιο για την παιδεία.
Ψηφίστηκε το για την παιδεία νομοσχέδιο.
check.answer: Ψηφίστηκε το νομοσχέδιο για την παιδεία.
check.why: Headline style: verb first, long subject last.

check.q: "The residents had been asking for these changes for years." (changes as topic)
check.answer: Τις αλλαγές αυτές τις ζητούσαν εδώ και χρόνια οι κάτοικοι.
check.why: Topic object first and doubled; the heavy new subject last.

check.q: Rewrite so that **η μείωση αυτή** is the topic: Οι αναλυτές αποδίδουν τη μείωση αυτή στον τουρισμό.
check.answer: Τη μείωση αυτή οι αναλυτές την αποδίδουν στον τουρισμό.
accept: Τη μείωση αυτή την αποδίδουν οι αναλυτές στον τουρισμό.
check.why: Front the object and double it with την.

title: Word order, topic and focus
blurb: Why Greek can say the same sentence in five orders, and how each order changes what is new, what is known and what is stressed.

intro.p: Greek marks subject and object by case (**ο σκύλος** nominative, **τον σκύλο** accusative), so it does not need word order to tell you who did what. Word order is free to do another job: it shows **what the sentence is about** (the topic, already known) and **what is new or contrasted** (the focus). English does this mainly with stress and with constructions such as "It was ... that". Greek does it by moving words and by adding a weak pronoun that "doubles" the object.
This guide starts with the neutral orders, then shows how fronting, doubling and stress change the message, and ends with the order inside the noun phrase and the fine points of written style.
